content.title: Authors' Response to Reviewer FpUc (Part 1)
content.comment:
Dear Reviewer,

Thank you for your detailed responses and reviews. Here are our answers to your comments and questions.

**STRENGTH AND WEAKNESSES**

**Q1. The methodology: $\mathcal{L}{contrastive}$ has no mention; which latent distribution is employed.** Regarding the $\mathcal{L}{contrastive}$ notation, we thank the reviewer for noting this out. In fact, $\mathcal{L}{contrastive}$ is $\mathcal{L}{nce}$. We made the correction in Algorithm 1 of the rebuttal revision to clarify the detail.

Regarding the latent distribution, we follow prior works [1-3] to use the linear layer to encode the BOW input x into the prior mean µ and standard deviation vectors σ, then define the latent distribution to the normal distribution $\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$ parameterized by those vectors.

**Q2. Pseudocode: where is H utilized, where is h' defined?** We thank the reviewer for pointing this out. Indeed, it should be $\mathbf{h}' = \phi(\mathbf{z}'{\kappa_{1}}, ..., \mathbf{z}'{\kappa_{K}})$ and $s_{i, j} = \frac{H^T_{i} H_{j}} {|| H^T_{i} || . || H^T_{i} ||} / τ$. We have corrected the details in the rebuttal revision.

**Q3. Topic diversity is ignored.** In our work, we follow a long line of topic modeling research [3-8] which use only coherence-based and classification metrics to evaluate topic quality. However, we agree that taking into account topic diversity (TD) [16] might construct better evaluation, and re-ran experiments to estimate TD. From the below tables denoting the experiment on 20NG and IMDb datasets, we can see that topics generated by set-based contrastive topic models exhibit more diversity and better avoid the topic collapse problem. Results on other datasets agree with our observation, which we have added to Table 2 and 3 in the rebuttal revision.

NTM|0.283 ± 0.004|0.734 ± 0.009|

NTM + CL|0.332 ± 0.006|0.853 ± 0.005|
Our Model|0.340 ± 0.005|0.913 ± 0.019|

IMDb|NPMI - C = 50|TD - C = 50 
|:---:|:---:|:---:|
NTM|0.170 ± 0.008|0.777 ± 0.021
ETM|0.174 ± 0.001|0.805 ± 0.019
DVAE|0.183 ± 0.004|0.836 ± 0.010  
BATM|0.065 ± 0.008|0.619 ± 0.016
W-LDA|0.136 ± 0.007|0.692 ± 0.016

NTM + CL|0.191 ± 0.004|0.857 ± 0.010
Our Model|0.200 ± 0.007|0.916 ± 0.008

**Q4. It is not entirely clear how the negative sampling is done.** As indicated in Lnce in Algorithm 1, since we have N = BP/K sets, for set $i$, we consider all sets $j ≠ i, 1 ≤ j ≤ N$ as negative samples. Therefore, we do not specify any particular negative sampling strategy to stochastically draw negative samples, which makes our method simpler than [3].

**Q5. There is no indication of whether the improvement is the result of a different sampling strategy from NTM + CL.** Thanks for your comment. Our work concentrates on a more general case of contrastive learning for neural topic models, which is the set-based approach. Hence, sampling strategy might be related, but out of scope. However, to expand the work, we followed your comment to compare our Embedding-based Sampling (ES) with Word-based Sampling (WS) in [3] to create positive and negative documents, which we leverage to construct document sets for our set-based contrastive loss. Below results on 20NG and IMDb demonstrate that there is no significant difference with respect to sampling methods. We added those experiments to Appendix G of the rebuttal revision. 

|20NG|C = 50| |C = 200| |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|

NTM+CL|0.332 ± 0.006|0.775 ± 0.008|0.277 ± 0.003|0.799 ± 0.009
Our Model (WS)|0.349 ± 0.005|0.909 ± 0.020|0.289 ± 0.004|0.902 ± 0.004
Our Model (ES)|0.340 ± 0.005|0.913 ± 0.019|0.291 ± 0.003|0.905 ± 0.004

|IMDb|C = 50| |C = 200| |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| |NPMI|TD|NPMI|TD|
NTM+CL|0.191 ± 0.004|0.857 ± 0.010 |0.186 ± 0.002|0.856 ± 0.012
Our Model (WS)|0.198 ± 0.009|0.914 ± 0.006|0.195 ± 0.001|0.888 ± 0.012
Our Model (ES)|0.200 ± 0.007|0.916 ± 0.008|0.197 ± 0.003|0.892 ± 0.007

**Q6. Since then, newer baselines have been established (DVAE and ETM) and are validated through human evaluations.** Thank you for your suggestion. We have chosen to compare our approach with the up-to-date state-of-the-art methods in the paper [2-4, 12]. Following your recommendation, we additionally ran the training of ETM [16] and DVAE [17] models on datasets for $C = 50$ and $C = 200$, and noted the NPMI score and topic diversity (TD) in Q3 above.

As can be observed, our method outperforms previous topic models, which proves the merit of the proposed set-based contrastive approach. We added the above results to the rebuttal revision of the paper.

content.title: Authors' Response to Reviewer Kyjc
content.comment:
Dear Reviewer,

Thank you very much for your feedback. Here are our responses.

**STRENGTH AND WEAKNESSES**

**Q1. Experimental work (number of datasets, evaluation methods) is poor.** We believe there is some misunderstanding of the scope of this work. The goal of this paper is to resolve the problem of overwhelming mutual information in current contrastive neural topic models. Therefore, we follow the experiment protocol in the thorough topic modeling literature of recent relevant papers [3-8] to conduct empirical studies on the chosen datasets and focus upon common-usage relevant coherence-based and classification-based metrics. We would like to re-emphasize that we are not aiming to solve all shortcomings of current Neural Topic models as stated in the SURVEY paper, so we did not conduct experiments on some irrelevant datasets or evaluation metrics. 

However, following your feedback, we have performed additional experiments on two datasets Yahoo Answer [18] and AG News [18], and utilized one additional metric, Topic Diversity (TD) [16] to report the results as follows:

|Yahoo Answers|NPMI - C = 50|TD - C = 50| 
|:---:|:---:|:---:|
|NTM|0.290 ± 0.003|0.897 ± 0.012|
|ETM|0.207 ± 0.001|0.808 ± 0.017|
|DVAE|0.319 ± 0.001|0.932 ± 0.014|
|BATM|0.247 ± 0.004|0.883 ± 0.019|
|W-LDA|0.222 ± 0.004|0.821 ± 0.008|
|SCHOLAR|0.327 ± 0.005|0.936 ± 0.019|
|SCHOLAR + BAT|0.328 ± 0.005|0.940 ± 0.020|
|NTM + CL|0.334 ± 0.002|0.954 ± 0.004|
|**Our Model**|**0.348** ± **0.004**|**0.988** ± **0.003**|

|AG News|NPMI - C = 50|TD - C = 50 |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|
|NTM|0.197 ± 0.015|0.729 ± 0.007|
|ETM|0.204 ± 0.004|0.736 ± 0.006|
|DVAE|0.271 ± 0.016|0.850 ± 0.013|
|BATM|0.256 ± 0.019|0.754 ± 0.008|
|W-LDA|0.270 ± 0.033|0.844 ± 0.014|
|SCHOLAR|0.278 ± 0.024|0.886 ± 0.007|
|SCHOLAR + BAT|0.272 ± 0.027|0.859 ± 0.008|
|NTM + CL|0.279 ± 0.025|0.890 ± 0.007|
|**Our Model**|**0.325** ± **0.012**|**0.934** ± **0.012**|

We can see that neural topic models aided by set-based contrastive learning still produce more coherent and diverse topics, which proves its efficiency and robustness. We inserted the above results to Table 3 and 12 in the rebuttal revision.

**Q2. Comparative methods are poor.** We also did more extensive experiments with other frameworks, i.e. ETM [16] and DVAE [17] on 20NG and IMDb datasets. In the below table, we denote our experiment results, which demonstrate that set-based contrastive learning does improve neural topic models better than previous baselines. We added the results to Table 2 and 3 in the rebuttal revision.

|20NG|C = 50| |C = 200| |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| |NPMI|TD|NPMI|TD|
|ETM|0.305 ± 0.006|0.776 ± 0.022|0.264 ± 0.002|0.623 ± 0.002|
|DVAE|0.320 ± 0.005|0.824 ± 0.017|0.269 ± 0.003|0.786 ± 0.005|
|**Our Model**|**0.340** ± **0.005**|**0.913** ± **0.019**|**0.291** ± **0.003**|**0.905** ± **0.004**|


|IMDb|C = 50| |C = 200| |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
|ETM |0.174 ± 0.001|0.805 ± 0.019|0.168 ± 0.001|0.687 ± 0.007|
|DVAE|0.183 ± 0.004|0.836 ± 0.010|0.173 ± 0.006|0.739 ± 0.005|
|**Our Model**|**0.200** ± **0.007**|**0.916** ± **0.008**|**0.197** ± **0.003**|**0.892** ± **0.007**|

**Q3. The basic idea is common in recent topic model papers.** We hope to better clarify the ideas in our paper and other topic modeling works. There are TWO fundamental differences between our work and recent topic modeling papers involving data fitting of pretrained language models (PLMs) [4, 13-15].

Firstly, while their works include a process to pretrain their models on a LARGE-SCALE upstream dataset before finetuning, we only train our framework upon the topic modeling dataset.

Secondly, whereas their methods aim to improve topic models via incorporating EXTERNAL signals from PLMs, we aim to polish mutual information extracted from INTERNAL documents of topic modeling datasets.

**CLARITY, QUALITY, NOVELTY, AND REPRODUCIBILITY**

**Which NPMI was used?** Regarding the NPMI score, we follow previous works [2-4, 9] to retrieve the top 10 words, estimate the NPMI score of every topic, then calculate the topics’ mean value. As pointed out by [9, 10] that evaluation using held-out documents does not necessarily correlate with human judgement of topic coherence, we utilize the testing split of each dataset as the reference corpus for NPMI estimation. We thank the reviewer for noting this out and inserted the details to the rebuttal revision.

**How were K and P in Sct 5.2 set?** In the paper, we experimented with different values of $K$ and $P$ in section 5.4. Subsequently, we extract the hyperparameters of the best results based on Figure 2 and 3 to include in Table 2, in particular $(K, P) = (4, 8)$ for 20NG and Wiki datasets, and $(K, P) = (3, 8)$ for the IMDb dataset. We made our choices clearer by inserting the details to Table 7 in Appendix E of the rebuttal revision.

content.title: Authors' Response to Reviewer PenD
content.comment:
Dear Reviewer,

Thank you for your insightful comments and feedback. We are happy that you found our paper interesting. Here are our answers to your questions and comments.

**STRENGTH AND WEAKNESSES**

**Although the performance of different poolings are analyzed. It might also be reasonable to use other approaches.** Regarding the pooling method, our intuition is that the operation should be able to extract notable features so that sets can be well-represented, which would make the discrimination task among them easier, and lead us to choose MaxPooling as the main aggregation function. To validate our assumption, we compare our choice with two additional pooling methods, MinPooling and Pooling with Sliced-Wasserstein Embedding (PSWE) [11]. MinPooling does provide the worst performance, while our choice of MaxPooling outperforms other pooling operations, which corroborates our intuition. Below we combine the results with those in the Appendix C.

|Method|C = 50|C = 200|
|:---:|:---:|:---:|
|MinPooling|0.190 ± 0.005|0.186 ± 0.004|
|MeanPooling|0.194 ± 0.006|0.195 ± 0.010|
|SumPooling|0.191 ± 0.007|0.188 ± 0.005|
|GAP|0.197 ± 0.003|0.196 ± 0.005|
|FSP|0.199 ± 0.004|0.195 ± 0.007|
|PSWE|0.194 ± 0.006|0.191 ± 0.003|
|MaxPooling|0.200 ± 0.007|0.197 ± 0.003|

**It can be more interesting to see the advantage of constructing sets based on input over based on hidden features.**
Thank you for your suggestion. We agree that it would be interesting to compare input-based and hidden features-based set construction, and will explore this direction in future research.

**CLARITY, QUALITY, NOVELTY, AND REPRODUCIBILITY**

**Maybe a typo here: In theorem 2: 't(y_j)=y_j'.** In fact, it should be 't(x_j)=y_j'. We thank the reviewer for pointing this out. We have corrected it in the rebuttal revision.

**Not clear about the details of NPMI score.** Regarding the NPMI score, we follow previous works [2-4, 9] to retrieve the top 10 words, estimate the NPMI score of every topic, then calculate the topics’ mean value. As pointed out by [9, 10] that evaluation using held-out documents does not necessarily correlate with human judgement of topic coherence, we utilize the testing split of each dataset as the reference corpus for NPMI estimation. We thank the reviewer for noting this out and added the detail to the rebuttal revision.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper proposes two improvements to neural topic models (NTMs) with contrastive loss. 

Firstly, it proposes to use set-based contrastive learning by dividing instances in a batch randomly into batches and using contrastive learning between the sets. It shows that by using set contrastive learning, the model can focus less on low-level features, but focus more on the common features within the sets. A set can also be seen as hard negatives because the same document can appear in multiple sets. 

Secondly, the paper proposes using multi-objective optimization to jointly optimize the contrastive loss and the ELBO loss. It argues that this can better optimize the loss without much manual tuning.

Experiments show that the proposed approach can improve the neural topic model performance.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength: The paper proposes an interesting extension for NTM using set-based contrastive learning. The finding is supported both theoretically and experimentally. Multi-objective optimization also improves the performance in ablation studies.

Weakness: The effect of the multi-objective optimization is mostly only supported by empirical evidence (Table 4). But the improvement is mild w.r.t simply use \alpha=0.5 (equal weight between contrastive loss and ELBO). There are many methods for optimizing many losses together (like those in Table 4) and the findings here might not generalize well to other datasets.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is nicely written and easy to read. Set-based contrastive learning for NTMs is novel.

The code is not included in the submission.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper builds on work by Nguyen and Luu 2021.  They combine an ELBO objective (to model the data) with a contrastive learning objective (to improve the representation).  The contrastive loss is built on small sets of examples.  Language models are used to apply word expansion when mapping a document to the word set input the the topic model, which is efficient.  They compare with a few recent-ish neural topic models.  Experiments are done on 20NG, IMDb and a small Wiki subset.  Evaluation uses NPMI and classification error.  Ablation tests are done as well.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
+ general idea of the multi-task loss is good
+ clear formulation and well written

Weaknesses:
+ experimental work (evaluation methods) could be improved
+ comparative methods are poor, in particular none done against language model methods
+ the basic idea (trading off data fitting with representation, for instance fit to a BERT language model) is common in recent topic model papers

Removed with update of paper.
+ some aspects of experimental work unclear (at least, I didn't locate) like setting of K and P in Sct 5.2
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
This is a well written paper.
But some of the experimental details are unclear.
(1)  which NPMI was used? they can be used with different dictionary data (building baseline stats) or use the training collection itself, each can give quite different answers.
(2)  how were K and P in Sct 5.2 set?
content.summary_of_the_review:
The original experimental work was inadequate for a mature field like Neural Topic models.  See for instance the survey paper at IJCAI 2021.  Given the huge number of methods, with many more published yearly, a small empirical study (3 data sets and two evaluation metrics) is not sufficient.   

On the plus side, the authors ended up doing good empirical work in their revision, although they still failed to include any of the many new models since 2021 in their comparison, particularly those using language models. Many models have now been tested, but they are older models.  Several of these new methods fix the LM and don't do any fine-tuning.  The authors have a particularly cost effective way of using older language models.

The authors also missed the complexity of NPMI evaluation: the reference corpus makes a big difference and the original method used a larger corpus, e.g., a news set or Wikipedia to compute word stats for NPMI is good when the topic model is run on news data. In this case, the word stats for NPMI is not built on the topic model's train/test data.

In the response, the authors say the goal of the paper is "to resolve the problem of overwhelming mutual information in current contrastive neural topic models". This is particular detail about a particular style of method and not an adequate goal for a quality venue. If the new method doesn't also hold up against other recent methods empirically, it should be relegated to a workshop because it doesn't offer substantial benefit to the field, rather it shows promise in improving a particular method.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This work proposes a set-based contrastive learning method for neural topic models, where the positives/negatives are constructed as sets rather than instances. To balance the influence of ELBO and contrastive loss, they apply MMO to find the Pareto stationary solution.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength: 1. They provide interesting examples and intuition to point out the limitation of instance-based discrimination for contrastive learning in NTM, as well as the necessity to balance the two losses. Then propose the solution, set-based contrastive learning and MMO. The process is logical and reasonable; 2. They show the advantage of their set-based discrimination which meets hard negative sampling and also has lower chance of semantic collapse, this is interesting; 3. They further show theoretical proof that their set-based contrastive method can capture common features among multiple inputs. 


Weakness: 1. When aggregating the set's representation, the choice of pooling operation is not clear. Although the performance of different poolings are analyzed. It might also be reasonable to use other approaches; 2. The advantage of set-based over instance-based contrastive learning is well illustrated, while it can be more interesting to see the advantage of constructing sets based on input over based on hidden features.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper addresses the concerns with the existing contrastive setting for topic modeling. Since contrastive learning is based on mutual information, the authors suggest that two main challenges arise for neural topic models. First, Immediate discrimination could focus on low mutual features (e.g., the number of nonzero entries and the ratio of maximum to minimum frequency). Second, since the contrastive target has a regulating effect of improving the generalization of hidden representations, generalizable but inefficient features for topic modeling might emerge, especially when the amount of mutual information exceeds the minimum sufficient statistics (e.g., the discrimination task might go beyond mutual topics to encode the joint existence of peculiar words or phrases) 

In their study, the authors hypothesize that useful features should be shared among input documents. For example, if the model is to capture the topic of sports, it must recognize the common sports topic in multiple documents. Intuitively, such shared semantics define sufficient information to encourage topic models to acquire effective features, and the learned representations should reflect multi-sample motivation.

Hence, there is a need to control the encoding of the contrastive objective to balance the influence of mutual information on the training of the neural topic model. To this end, the authors propose a set-based contrastive learning method for neural topic models using the concept of learning representations for multiple samples. 

The contrastive topic modeling is explicitly presented as a gradient-based multi-objective optimization to achieve a stationary Pareto solution that mitigates the effects of multiple objectives on updating the topic model parameters.

Their experiments show that the proposed framework is consistent and competitive with other baselines on topic coherence and downstream tasks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
# Strengths:

- A novel contrastive framework for topic modeling.
- Clear illustration of the limitations of existing contrastive learning in topic models.
- A sound theoretical solution to the limitations is presented.
- Overall good results.

# Weaknesses:

- The methodology is poorly explained (for ex. $\mathcal{L}_{contrastive}$ which is mentioned in the Pseudo code has no mention in the text; which latent distribution is employed.)
- Pseudo code in itself is not clear (where is $H$ utilized?; where is $h^{'}$ defined? etc.)
- Topic evaluation is only coherence based and topic diversity is ignored. What if there is a mode collapse with the presented approach?
- It is not entirely clear how the negative sampling is done.
- There is no indication of whether the improvement is the result of a different sampling strategy from NTM + CL.
- The compared NTM baseline is from 2016. Since then, newer baselines have been established (DVAE and ETM) and are validated through human evaluations (By Hoyle et al.)
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
# Clarity

The illustration of the limitations of existing contrastive learning in topic models is very clear. The explanation and description of the method itself needs to be improved though.

# Quality

The idea is to change the sampling step in the contrastive neural topic model. It is clear how the positive sampling is performed, but the negative sampling is not explained well. Some of the equations are not explained in the text. Therefore the quality of the writing needs to be improved. Also the experimental comparison does not include common state-of-the-art neural topic models.

# Novelty

The framework of proposing a new sampling step is novel.

# Reproducibility

Code is not submitted with the paper, some parts are unclear, so it cannot be reproduced


Minor issues:

- Table 4 is out of bound.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Valid limitations of contrastive settings in neural topic models are presented. The solution discussed is theoretically sound. But, the description lacks clarity. Following the description and replicating methodology is difficult since bits and pieces are missing. The evaluation is also not complete. Therefore the paper cannot be accepted at this stage.

UPDATE:
In light of authors significant additions, I increase my score and am happy with the paper to be accepted.

content.title: Multi-Sample Contrastive Neural Topic Model as Multi-Task Learning
content.abstract: Recent representation learning approaches to polish global semantics of neural topic models optimize the weighted linear combination of the evidence lower bound (ELBO) of the log-likelihood and the discriminative objective that contrasts instance pairings. However, contrastive learning on the individual level might capture noisy mutual information that is irrelevant to the topic modeling task. Moreover, there is a potential conflict between the ELBO loss that memorizes input details for better reconstruction quality, and the contrastive term which attempts to generalize representations among inputs. To address the issues, we firstly hypothesize that useful features should be shared among multiple input samples. For that reason, we propose a novel set-based contrastive learning method for neural topic models to employ the concept of multi-sample representation learning. Secondly, because the solution of the linear combination approach might not satisfy all objectives when they compete, we explicitly cast contrastive topic modeling as gradient-based multi-objective optimization, with the goal of achieving a Pareto stationary solution. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our framework consistently produces higher-performing neural topic models in terms of topic coherence and downstream performance.
